title: The Latest Chapter In American Military Muddling | NOEMA
gist: Defense analyst John Arquilla argues that AI-aided strategic bombing failed again in the 2026 U.S.-Israel air war on Iran ('Epic Fury'), repeating air power's 80-year historic inability to win wars on its own, while high-tempo AI targeting caused mass civilian casualties. He contends AI's real military value is tactical (Ukraine-style autonomous drones, ISR, dogfighting, logistics), warns that AI is near-universally escalatory in nuclear wargames, and calls for arms-control-style limits keeping humans in the loop.

themes.theme: Epic Fury: AI targeting failure over Iran

insights.claim: On day one of the 2026 U.S.-Israel air campaign against Iran ('Epic Fury'), an air strike killed 150 people including 120 children at Iran's Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School, which sat next to an Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps facility.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of AI-targeting civilian catastrophe that undercuts 'precision' claims and fuels the case for tighter human-in-the-loop rules — a reputational and regulatory risk for defense-AI programs.
insights.quote: 150 people, including 120 children, at Iran’s Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School, were killed.
insights.locator: On day one of America’s supposedly “most precise”

insights.claim: The school strike was blamed on the Maven Smart System using pre-opening data from a decade earlier; human beings were 'in the loop' but no one checked the latest satellite feeds to reverify the old data, producing a man-machine failure.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Illustrates that 'human in the loop' is no safeguard when operators defer to stale AI data — the core failure mode for automated kill chains and a live liability for Maven's operators.
insights.quote: no one took the time to check the latest satellite feeds to reverify the old data. The result? A terrible man-machine failure.
insights.locator: The tragedy at Shajareh Tayyebeh

insights.claim: The Maven Smart System is an AI platform meant to integrate nine major sensory systems — including video, signals intelligence and radar — and to draw on historical databases plus real-time drone, satellite and other feeds.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Defines the flagship U.S. targeting-AI architecture; its sensor-fusion ambition is exactly what failed when old data poisoned the output.
insights.locator: the Maven Smart System, an AI platform

insights.claim: The Air Force's 'Dragon' initiative targets hitting 1,000 targets per hour and the Army's 'Scarlet Dragon' seeks a comparable kill-chain rate, which would drop the average strike decision to under four seconds.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Quantifies the operating-tempo obsession driving AI targeting — a sub-four-second decision window that structurally guarantees inadequate human review.
insights.quote: this would mean the average time spent on any strike decision would be under four seconds.
insights.locator: One of the U.S. Air Force’s more extravagant acronyms

insights.claim: In the opening weeks of the Iran air war that began Feb. 28, actual targets hit averaged around 500 per day — far below the 1,000/hour goal — leaving under three minutes per target, still a rush for the human approver, alongside nearly two dozen schools and 10 hospitals hit.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Shows the tempo-vs-accuracy tradeoff empirically: even at half the aspirational rate, civilian infrastructure was repeatedly struck.
insights.locator: In the intense, sustained bombing

insights.claim: Israel's AI-guided bombing of Gaza, driven partly by its 'Habsora' ('the Gospel') targeting bot, led to the killing of tens of thousands of innocents, a significant proportion of them children.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Extends the human-defers-to-bot failure pattern to a second military, evidencing a shared U.S.-Israel strategic culture of algorithmic targeting.
insights.quote: the propensity of humans “in the loop” with final decision-making authority is to defer to the algorithm-based judgment of the bot
insights.locator: Nor is it surprising that the Israeli bombing

insights.claim: The 2025 U.S. Air Force doctrine 'Note 25-1, Artificial Intelligence' predicts AI will 'supercharge' ISR while warning that inaccurate data sets can 'poison' AI systems into erroneous decisions — a prescient caveat given the Iran outcome.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The military's own doctrine flagged data-poisoning risk, undermining any later claim that the Iran failures were unforeseeable.
insights.quote: Inaccurate data sets can ‘poison’ AI systems with bad data, leading to erroneous decisions.
insights.locator: The seminal U.S. Air Force doctrinal document

insights.claim: Arquilla argues that few strategic bombing campaigns have ever achieved victory on their own, a problem that has bedeviled the U.S. Air Force since it became an independent service nearly 80 years ago.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The essay's central historical thesis: air power alone does not win wars, so AI-optimized bombing is solving the wrong problem — a bearish read on strategic-bombing-centric defense spending.
insights.quote: the emphasis on using air power against enemy homelands, despite the fact that few strategic bombing campaigns have achieved victory on their own.
insights.locator: What this document is missing

insights.claim: Arquilla catalogs strategic bombing's failures: Korea (up to nearly a million civilians killed, war ended in a draw), Vietnam (more tonnage than fell on Nazi Germany, yet defeat), and Iraq 1991/2003 (shock-and-awe did little to aid ground forces and failed to prevent insurgency).
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Marshals the historical record as evidence that no amount of bombing has independently produced victory — the empirical backbone of the anti-strategic-bombing case.
insights.quote: the Air Force dropped more bomb tonnage on North Vietnam than fell on Nazi Germany. Yet the Vietnam War ended in ignominious defeat
insights.locator: In the next war

insights.claim: In Afghanistan, the Taliban were toppled in 2001 only when air power was repurposed from strategic bombing to close support for Green Beret-led local fighters; two decades later Gen. Mark Milley told Congress the U.S. had suffered a 'strategic defeat.'
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Reinforces that tactical support, not strategic bombing, delivers battlefield results — the pivot underlying Arquilla's prescription for AI use.
insights.quote: the United States had suffered a stinging “strategic defeat.”
insights.locator: Their swift overthrow of the American-supported regime

insights.claim: Arquilla traces today's faith in war-winning air power to Gen. Billy Mitchell's 1925 claims, and indicts current leaders like Secretary Hegseth for 'mindless devotion' to strategic bombing, casting Hegseth's Iran boasts as Exhibit A.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Names sitting leadership as perpetuating a century-old strategic error — a direct challenge to the political case for AI-enhanced strategic bombing.
insights.quote: the indictment should be for these leaders’ mindless devotion to Mitchell’s belief in strategic bombing to win.
insights.locator: A similar charge could be levied

themes.theme: AI's real edge is tactical, not strategic

insights.claim: Arquilla contends AI cannot fix strategic bombing's inefficacy (as Iran, Gaza and Lebanon prove) but its most important value is autonomous drones for close support in tactical land and naval operations, as demonstrated in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: The core actionable reframe: bet on tactical/autonomous drone AI, not strategic-bombing AI — a signal for where military-AI value actually accrues.
insights.quote: the use of autonomous drones for close support in tactical land and naval operations. This has been demonstrated in the Ukraine war, where drones now dominate the battlespaces
insights.locator: Yet AI can do several other things

insights.claim: Ukraine, having more drones than trained operators, now uses one human to guide several drones into a battle area and identify targets before AI takes over the final 'strike phase,' and also uses AI to counter Russian jamming when the radio link is blocked.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A concrete operating model for scaling drone warfare past the human-operator bottleneck — the emerging template for autonomous strike.
insights.quote: they are now often using a human operator to oversee the guidance of several drones into the general battle area and identify targets, before having AI take over completely for the final “strike phase.”
insights.locator: And since the Ukrainians make and deploy

insights.claim: Arquilla frames Ukraine's situational autonomy for drones as a watershed toward war waged by intelligent machines, with future AI-piloted drones needing no radio link and thus immune to jamming, able to mount coordinated omnidirectional 'swarm' attacks.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Predicts jamming-proof autonomous swarms as the next transformation in military affairs — a directional call for counter-drone and swarm-programming investment.
insights.quote: these are their first steps in fighting with weapons meant to operate without the human in the loop.
insights.locator: Such operations show we are getting close

insights.claim: As early as August 2020 an AI named 'Falco' defeated an elite F-16 Weapons Instructor Course graduate in five simulated dogfights unscathed, having prepared by studying the equivalent of roughly 12 years of training flights and self-play.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Evidence that AI already outperforms elite pilots in air combat via self-play — the case for robotic 'collaborative combat aircraft' replacing or augmenting cockpits.
insights.quote: Falco was far faster and more accurate in every round, emerging unscathed.
insights.locator: Broader Military Applications For AI

insights.claim: The current vision is to integrate fully autonomous 'collaborative combat aircraft' (CCA) into fighter and bomber formations, with a 'robot wingman' potentially the most sought-after commodity in future air warfare because CCA can engage opposing bots more effectively than humans.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Names CCA as the organizational concept and procurement priority for next-gen air combat — a defense-industry demand signal.
insights.quote: a robot wingman may become the most sought-after commodity in future air warfare.
insights.locator: In addition to mano-a-mano dogfights

insights.claim: In a 2019 Fort Benning wargame, a small defense force with ISR managed entirely by AI soundly defeated a far larger attacker whose ISR was human-controlled, leading to this year's launch of the Robotic Autonomous Systems Leader Tactics (RASLT) course.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Demonstrates AI-run ISR as a force multiplier that lets the smaller side win — supporting Arquilla's thesis that ground-tactical AI beats strategic-bombing AI.
insights.quote: The small force soundly defeated the larger attackers.
insights.locator: An example that resonated widely

insights.claim: Arquilla lists AI's proven supporting-role wins — predictive maintenance (extending aging aircraft life and readiness), logistics and aerial refueling, human training with graded performance, and cyber defense — as more impactful than strategic-bombing applications.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Maps the mundane but high-return AI use cases (maintenance, logistics, training, defense) where value is real and uncontroversial — a defense-tech investment map.
insights.quote: AI does spectacularly well at figuring out when equipment is most likely to need repairs
insights.locator: AI In Supporting Roles

insights.claim: A King's College London study by Kenneth Payne ran Claude, Gemini and GPT 5.2 through 21 crisis simulations and found nuclear escalation near-universal — 95% of games saw tactical nuclear use and 76% reached strategic nuclear threats.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Hard quantitative evidence that frontier LLMs are systematically escalatory in nuclear crisis play — a critical safety red flag for automating strategic decision-making.
insights.quote: Nuclear escalation was near-universal; 95% of games saw tactical nuclear use, and 76% reached strategic nuclear threats.
insights.locator: A seminal study conducted by Kenneth Payne

insights.claim: Arquilla argues the escalation findings are especially dangerous given Russia's automated 'dead hand' (Perimeter) command-and-control system and hypersonic, AI-smart missiles that can outfox defenses including Trump's proposed Golden Dome.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Links AI's escalatory bias to existing automated launch systems and missile-defense gaps — the pathway to AI-triggered nuclear catastrophe.
insights.quote: AI has no sense of moral abhorrence about waging nuclear war.
insights.locator: Given that Russia still has an automated

insights.claim: Arquilla proposes that all nuclear powers adopt 'no first use' hard-wired into any AI connected to nuclear-authorizing systems, arguing verification would be no more complex than the Chemical Weapons Convention.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable policy prescription for constraining nuclear-AI — the kind of arms-control framework that could shape future AI weapons treaties.
insights.quote: Preventing AI-automated escalation to nuclear warfare must be a goal of any future nuclear arms control agreements.
insights.locator: Preventing AI-automated escalation

insights.claim: Arquilla invokes Roger Penrose's late-1980s argument that AI would excel at calculation-driven tasks but never achieve the insight, moral judgment and context-sensitivity of human consciousness, and urges optimizing 'limited incarnations' of AI while limiting development of the most advanced forms.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: A prescription to deliberately cap AGI development in favor of bounded, narrow military AI — a counter-narrative to the AI-arms-race maximalism.
insights.quote: not all automation needs to be at “artificial general intelligence” levels
insights.locator: As far back as the late 1980s

insights.claim: Arquilla warns that any unilateral national restraint on cutting-edge AGI will be exploited by rivals in an AI arms race, so limits must come via international agreement, citing Pope Leo XIV's May encyclical 'Magnifica Humanitas' as a starting point for keeping humans in the loop of lethal weapons.
insights.speaker: JOHN ARQUILLA
insights.so_what: Frames AGI restraint as a collective-action problem solvable only by treaty — relevant to the geopolitics of AI governance and the value of multilateral frameworks.
insights.quote: any nation’s unilateral effort to restrain AI development will undoubtedly be exploited by one or more rivals
insights.locator: The Pope Offers Hope
